10 Electrostatics

What is the nature of charge?

Contents

  • Electric Charge

  • Electric Force

  • Electric Fields

Curious phenomena

The ancients knew that certain materials had attractive properties

Amber \, rubbed with fur\, would cause very light objects to stick to it

__Lodestones __ exert magnetic attraction to iron

Greek for amber is “elektron” \, for which electricity has become named

Thales

626 - 545 BCE

That’s… a very big magnet

Englishman William Gilbert was the first to coin the term “ electric ”\, referring to the Greek

Compared electricity to magnetism \, exploring their differences and determining that Earth was a giant magnet

Explored why magnets always work\, but electricity must be prepared (thought it was effluvium )

William Gilbert

1544 - 1603 CE

What could go wrong?

Hashtag what the hecking

![bg left 60% drop-shadow](/img/0%20Lecture%20_%2010%20Electrostatics_2.png)

**Benjamin Franklin**  
1706 - 1790 CE

Did fly a  __kite__  on an overcast day\, lived to tell the tale \(others tried and suffered death\-related symptoms\)  

Demonstrated that  __lightning__  was a buildup of  __static__   __electricity__  

Thought electricity was a “fluid” that was  __transferred__  from one material to another  

Somewhat arbitrarily determined  __positives__  and  __negatives__  for charge

</div>

Franklin’s Contributions: The Law of Charges

Charges ( q ) exist in two forms: positives and negatives

Like charges repel; __opposite __ charges attract

Charge is conserved ; the net amount of electric charge produced in any (natural) process is zero

Charges in Atoms

In their default state\, atoms are electrically neutral

The number of protons is balanced by the number of electrons

Electrons are easily transferred between some atoms

Materials and Charge

When one atom has a greater affinity for electrons\, it can “ steal ” them from another

The buildup of electrons on one material and absence on the other results in unequal charges

The interaction between positive and negative charges results in an attractive force

“Quantum” charge

Careful experiments in the 19th and 20th centuries showed that charge is quantized

Charge always exists in pairs and is always in multiples of a fundamental unit of charge

This fundamental unit is symbolized by the letter _e _ and represents the precise charge of a single particle

The elementary charge

A proton is said to carry a charge of + e and an electron is said to carry a charge of - e

The value of _e _ has been determined experimentally to be

1.602176 x 10-19 C\, or Coulombs

We approximate this value\, called elementary charge \, as 1.6 x 10 -19 __ __C

Charges and masses of atomic particles

Table 1. Summary of charges and masses of atomic particles
Particle Charge (C) Mass (kg)
electron $-1.60E-19$ $9.109 \times 10^{-31}$
proton $+1.60E-19$ $1.673 \times 10^{-27}$
neutron 0 $1.675 \times 10^{-27}$

Conductors transfer charge

Materials in which charge flows freely are called conductors

Examples: metals\, some liquids

Conductors distribute charge through the material (and into others\, if able)

Insulators do not transfer charge

Materials through which charge does not flow are called insulators

Examples: glass\, rubber\, silk\, plastic

Insulators keep charges local

Semi- and superconductors

Semiconductors are materials which transfer charge at intermediate rates\, depending on their chemical composition

Superconductors are materials which transfer charge indefinitely when kept at very low temperatures

Charge can transfer by contact

Insulators can be charged by contact and the charges hold because the material does not transfer it readily to anything else

Conductors require being handled with an insulator to charge\, otherwise they just transfer the charge to the human body (which is a conductor)

Ground

Connecting a conductor to the Earth\, called grounding \, is a way of redirecting excess charge into a basically infinite sink for electrons

Grounding is done in both electrostatics and electric currents to protect people and devices from unexpected/unwanted flows of charge

Charge by induction

One charged\, insulating sphere imbalances the charge in another

A ground is attached to the second sphere\, allowing the electrons to leave the sphere and travel to earth

The ground is removed\, leaving an excess of positive charge in the second sphere

Me? Bourgeois? No, no

Military commander until the French Revolution

Was called to systematize measures after Revolution

Discovered the inverse square relationship between the distances of charges

Soon thereafter discovered a similar property of the magnetic force

Charles Augustin de Coulomb

1736 - 1806 CE

The Electric Force

Coulomb observed that two charged objects near each other experience acceleration

This acceleration is said to be due to the Electric Force

Coulomb observed that:

The closer two objects are together\, the greater is the force between them

The stronger the charge of the two objects\, the greater is the force between them

Measuring the force

Coulomb carefully measured the attractive force using a torsion balance

Two charges are separated \, one an insulating rod suspended by silk

The attraction of the two is measured when the rod twists \, and a reflected light wave measures the angle of the displacement

Coulomb’s Law

Coulomb’s Law describes the relationship between the electric force\, charges\, and distances between the charges

The force is proportionate to the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them

Coulomb’s Constant

Coulomb found a constant of proportionality relating the force strength to the charges and distances

We can estimate this as:

Coulomb’s Law and Newton’s Gravitation

Universal Constant

Product of Quantities

Inverse square (distances)

The electric force can be attractive or repulsive;

Gravity is only ever attractive

Quantifying charge

Coulomb (C) is the SI unit of electric charge

</section> The Coulomb is defined as the charge of a single subatomic particle,

The reason for this number relates to electrical current and the work of other Frenchmen

Coulomb (C) is the SI unit of electric charge

| __Name__ | __Symbol__ | __Conversion Factor__ | | :-: | :-: | :-: | | Millicoulomb | mC | $1\,mC = 10^{-3} \, C$ | | microcoulomb | μC | $1\,\mu C = 10^{-6} \, C$ | | nanocoulomb | nC | $1\,nC = 10^{-9} \,C$ |

Electric Fields

The fact that induction works without actually touching the two charged spheres together indicates that the electric force is a field force

The balloon-on-hair demonstration shows that the electric force is much stronger than the gravitational force

The concept of a field helps explain how forces __ can be exerted on objects at a __distance

Even Newton was hesitant about this concept in his maths

Electric fields can be thought as regions of space around a charged object

When another charged object enters the field\, forces of an electrical nature arise

The electric field strength can be calculated using a test charge\, q 0 placed near a second object with larger charge\, Q

Large test charges could redistribute charge in the source\, causing measurement errors

Test charges are assumed to be positive and relatively small in charge

The strength of a field

The electric field strength __ can be calculated using a __test charge \, q 0 placed near a second object with larger charge\, Q

Fields can interact with each other

Unequal charges can produce imbalanced fields

Placing charges in fields causes acceleration

If a field strength is proportional to distance and charge\, the force in the field is:

Acceleration of a particle of charge q and mass m in a field of strength E

Example 1 | Electrons of a hydrogen atom

The electron and proton of a hydrogen atom are separated\, on average\, by a distance of about 5.3x10-11 m. Find the magnitude of the electric force that each particle exerts on the other.

Holt, Sample A, p. 565 8.2x10-8 N

Wavelength = 1.31 m

Example 2 | A quantum tug-of-war

Three charges lie along a single axis. One charge\, q 1 _ =_ +15 μC\, is at x = 2.0 m and another\, q 2 _ =_ +6.0 μC \, is at the origin. At what point on the x-axis must q 3 _ _ be placed so that the resultant force on it is zero?

Holt, Sample C, p. 569 0.77 m

Wavelength = 1.31 m

Example 3 | Electric Field Strength

Two point charges are separated by a distance of 10.0 cm. One has a charge of -25 µC and the other +50 __µC. __

Determine the direction and magnitude of the electric field at a point\, P \, between the two charges that is 2.0 cm from the negative charge.

If an electron (mass = 9.11 x 10-31 kg) is placed at rest at point P and then released\, what will be its initial acceleration (direction and magnitude)?

Giancoli Example 16-8, pp. 455 6.3 x 108 N 1.1 x 1020 m/s2 toward the +50 µC charge
